description:
I'm an Erasmus Mundus robotics master's student with space robotics & GNC experience from CATEC (using SIL, Orekit, GMAT, Basilisk, MuJoCo).

I'm building a field-robotics style navigation project for Mars: layered NASA data, hazard-aware routes, and an interactive map for explorers/rovers. Goal: a competition-winning technical prototype.

Seeking: UI/UX devs, data visualization experts, planetary scientists, and robotics engineers (navigation/planning). Join to build a strong product and win!
summary:
A route across Mars is more than a line on a map: terrain changes how long a traverse takes, what tradeoffs a crew faces, and whether a plan includes a way home. Project XLR8 is an interactive, physics-coupled EVA route-planning application for Gale Crater. It combines Mars elevation data, thermal inertia, and radiation data with A* pathfinding and a Mars-adjusted walking-speed model.

Users can set start/destination points, add waypoints and hazard zones, and instantly compare distance-focused routes against physics-based safe routes. Crucially, XLR8 proves the value of robotic assistance: our "Rover Assist" mode drops the astronaut 1 km from the science target, reducing radiation exposure by 90% (from 140 μGy to 14 μGy) and cutting EVA time from 13 hours to 2.5 hours. With built-in return-path planning and real Curiosity imagery for visual context, XLR8 turns planetary data into actionable mission survival decisions.
details:
What it does & How it works:

Project XLR8 is a web-based route-planning prototype for a ~30 km × 30 km study area around Bradbury Landing in Gale Crater. It brings terrain visualization and physics-based route planning into one interactive map. Users select a start and destination, place waypoints, add hazard-exclusion zones, and compare route alternatives.

How route planning works:

The map displays hillshade and slope derived from Mars elevation data, plus a thermal-inertia layer. The planner runs A* search on a 50 m grid. Its distance-focused route minimizes distance subject to configured terrain barriers. Its weighted route also accounts for slope, a thermal-inertia-derived slip proxy, and modeled dose.

For walking segments, a Mars-adjusted Tobler model estimates speed from slope and gravity. The dose estimate applies a Curiosity RAD-derived measurement rate uniformly. Rover Assist models a fixed-speed pressurized rover route with a final walking approach, proving a 90% radiation reduction. A nearby-image feature finds cataloged Curiosity images associated with the selected location for visual surface context.

Technology & Source Code:

The project uses Python, FastAPI, A*, NumPy, Pandas, and Rasterio for the API, terrain processing, and planning; React, TypeScript, Vite, and Leaflet for the map interface. Source code is available at: https://github.com/Gaafoor/NASA_2026_MARS_Exploration
